content: Gabonese Forestry Code, Loi n. 016/01 of 20 December 2001 (as amended): Article 21 — logging concessions must apply Exploitation Forestiere a Faible Impact (EFIR, reduced-impact logging), including pre-felling inventories, skid trail planning, and directional felling to limit soil and residual stand damage. Article 22 — priority to local processing of timber on Gabonese territory; raw log export restrictions. Article 251 — development of local communities: obligations to involve and benefit populations adjacent to forest concessions (community forestry allocations, local employment, cooperative development). Non-compliance jeopardizes concession renewal. These articles anchor the corporate CSR (RSE) section of valorization plans: diverting residues to local cooperatives demonstrates Art. 251 community development and Art. 22 local transformation. Reference: loi_016_01.

FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) Principles 3 and 4: Principle 3 — Indigenous Peoples' Rights: the forest manager must identify and uphold indigenous and local communities' rights to land and resources, customary rights, and FPIC (free, prior and informed consent), and ensure community relations are maintained. Principle 4 — Community Relations and Workers' Rights: the enterprise and workers supporting local economic development, ensuring fair wages and safe conditions, and fostering community access to benefits. Operational indicators relevant to residue valorization: documented benefit-sharing with nearby cooperatives, local value-addition projects, and inclusion of non-timber forest product processing. FSC group certification can include residue-supply sub-projects (chips, bark) if traceability is maintained. Reference: fsc_p3_p4.

metadata.source: FSC Forest Stewardship Council Principles and Criteria v6

content: PEFC / PAFC (Pan-African Forest Certification): PAFC is the African endorsement of PEFC, relevant to Gabonese and Congo Basin certified operations. Certification criteria requiring corporate waste mitigation and socio-economic integration include: sustainable management of harvest residues (no open burning), contribution to local employment and skills transfer, and chain-of-custody for by-products. Certified companies can count cooperative residue-supply programs as evidence of continuous improvement objectives; energy briquettes and biochar produced from certified feedstock can carry the chain-of-custody label. Reference: pafc.

Paris Agreement Article 6 — avoided methane from residue diversion: open-air decomposition of moist forest residues under anaerobic conditions emits methane; diverting residue biomass to stable products (biochar carbon sequestration, mycelium boards, dried furniture wood, tannin extracts) avoids these emissions. Project accounting uses GWP100 = 28 (AR5 value; AR6 value 27.9 for fossil CH4, 27.2 including feedbacks). Default emission factor used by the engine: 0.05 kg CH4 per kg dry residue over a 5-year decomposition window (project default pending site-specific measurement). Biochar carbon stability (EBC: 50-80% of feedstock C retained >100 years) provides additional durable removals eligible under Article 6 corresponding adjustments when authorized by the host country (Gabon).

content: CITES Appendix II listing of key Gabonese/Congo Basin timbers: Pericopsis elata (Assamela / Afrormosia) has been listed in Appendix II since 1992, with Gabon operating under an annual export quota for sawn timber; Guibourtia spp. (Kevazingo / Bubinga group, incl. G. tessmannii, G. demeusei, G. pellegriniana) were listed in Appendix II at CoP18 (2019). Consequence for valorization: any residue stream that could be confused with regulated timber (offcuts, branch wood, sawdust of listed species) must preserve chain-of-custody, harvest documentation and location data, because CITES non-detriment findings and export permits attach to the species. Logging companies should segregate listed-species residues and log them separately in the traceability system; cooperatives must not accept listed-species feedstock without provenance documentation. Reference: cites_app2.

Gabon raw-log export prohibition: since 2010 Gabon has banned the export of unprocessed logs (reinforcing Loi n. 016/01 Article 22 on priority to local processing), with subsequent measures tightening controls on log exports and transforming the sector toward domestic sawmilling, veneer and plywood. The operational consequence is that harvesting residues (branches, stumps, bark, sawdust) are concentrated at local processing sites and landings rather than exported, making on-site residue valorization both logistically feasible and policy-aligned. Valorization plans that divert residues to local cooperatives directly support the local-transformation policy objective. Compliance evidence for CSRs includes volumes processed on national territory and residue-utilization rates. Reference: gabon_log_export_ban.

metadata.source: Gabon Loi 016/01 Art. 22 + 2010 log-export ban (Journal Officiel Gabon / ITTO)

content: Gabonese community forestry and benefit-sharing: Loi n. 016/01 (Articles 251-256) establishes the obligation to associate local communities with forest management and provides for community forest allocations, local employment and benefit-sharing around concessions. Community forests (forets communautaires) let village associations manage and valorize defined forest areas under a simplified management plan, and can serve as the legal vehicle for residue-processing cooperatives (biochar, briquettes, furniture, NTFP oils). For a CSR valorization plan, routing residues to a registered community cooperative is documentary evidence of Article 251 compliance and of FSC Principle 3/4 community relations. Benefit-sharing agreements should specify volumes, prices, and a share of end-product revenue to the community entity. Reference: gabon_community_forestry.

metadata.source: Gabon Loi 016/01 Art. 251-256 / community forest framework
